HEADLINE: Property database
TEXT: The Property Council of Australia has launched its free Data Room database providing more than 80 data sets across 12 categories with up-to-date global, national and state-level economic statistics, information on government taxes, infrastructure expenditure, occupancy rates, returns and values across the industry, as well as details on sustainability ratings, foreign investment sources and more. MATTHEW CRANSTON

HEADLINE: RMIT leasing deal
TEXT: Dexus has struck a major leasing deal with RMIT University at 222 Lonsdale Street in Melbourne. RMIT has leased 10,634 sq m across levels 5, 6 and 7 for a 15-year term, beginning in March 2020. As part of the deal, Dexus will upgrade the Lonsdale Street building and refurbish the amenities.The lease was secured 18 months ahead of the lease expiry for the current tenant, Sensis, in July 2019. NICK LENAGHAN

HEADLINE: Walker St sale
TEXT: The commercial building 123 Walker Street in North Sydney is on the market with price expectations of just under $20 million. The fully leased 1985 sq m property on a net annual rent income of $92,375 has 16 car spaces. CI Australia's Nick Lowry and Bevan Kenny are handling the expressions of interest sale for a private owner. SU-LIN TAN

HEADLINE: Biotech Sirtex agrees to $1.6b takeover deal
TEXT:
The board of biotechnology group Sirtex Medical has agreed to a $1.6 billion takeover offer from United States giant Varian Medical Systems, after receiving a number of takeover offers in late 2017. The all-cash offer is priced at $28 a share, a 49 per cent premium to the $18.83 price that Sirtex shares last traded at before they were suspended on Tuesday. Varian is listed on the New York Stock Exchange and has a market value of $US11.8 billion ($14.6 billion). Sirtex is best known for its technology to fight last-stage colorectal liver cancer.

Companies Report p19

HEADLINE: JB Hi-Fi defies the Amazon retail gloom
TEXT: Short-sellers in JB Hi-Fi are ducking for cover as shares in the consumer electronics retailer surge to near 12-month highs following a series of earnings upgrades. JB Hi-Fi is the third most shorted stock on the Australian Securities Exchange, with almost 15 per cent of shares sold short. Yet JB Hi-Fi has so far proved its doubters wrong, with the shares soaring more than 27 per cent since November to reach $28.91 yesterday. JB Hi-Fi shares fell more than 20 per cent last year amid fears it would be one of the retailers hardest hit by Amazon's entry. Companies p24

HEADLINE: Locked-out miners paid 'scab' bonuses
TEXT:
Exclusive | Glencore, the commodities giant, has been paying locked-out coal miners bonuses of up to $700 a week because of big productivity improvements driven by replacement "scab" workers. A three-year dispute at Glencore's Oaky Creek coal mine has left 175 miners locked out for 203 days, despite repeated attempts to break the deadlock. While Glencore is not paying the unionised miners a salary, the existing employment agreement allows for any production bonuses to be paid through a union-led strike or a company lock out.

News Report p3

Matthew Stevens p34

HEADLINE: Beijing behind property reshuffle
TEXT: This week's two big Australian property deals worth a collective $1.3 billion are the end result of Beijing's clampdown on the unrestrained spending by some of China's most high-profile companies on so-called "vanity" projects, such as flashy high-rises or entertainment companies. HNA Group sold its office tower at 1 York Street in Sydney to US private equity group Blackstone for $205 million and 24 hours later entertainment conglomerate Dalian Wanda announced the $1.13 billion sale of its Sydney and Gold Coast projects to China-backed developer Yuhu Group. Property Michael Smith p38

HEADLINE: Shorten 'war on business'
TEXT:
Labor has drawn the battle lines for a pre-election, cost-of-living contest by promising fatter pay packets through the reduction of employers' workplace bargaining rights and a boosted minimum wage, in contrast with the government's plan to cut company tax.

Prompting warnings from business he could jeopardise Australia's economic and jobs recovery by targeting industrial relations laws introduced by the previous Labor government, Bill Shorten flagged changes to enterprise bargaining laws to empower workers, and an increased minimum wage, possibly with the introduction of a so-called living wage to stop people falling below the bread line.

The Labor leader also vowed to go after private health insurers over their annual fee increases, labelling them "big multinationals" and "big profitable companies" whose business model was no longer acceptable.

And he promised to establish a federal anti-corruption watchdog - a National Integrity Commission - which he said was needed to restore faith in politics.

In shades of Kevin Rudd's 2007 pitch toward "working families" who were not feeling the benefit of a then-buoyant economy, Mr Shorten directed his core economic message to what he called the "left-behind society" trapped between by a rising cost of living and flat wages.

The ACTU has proposed a living wage set at 60 per cent of the median wage, which would see the current minimum wage of $695 a week jump to $852. Mr Shorten did not commit to the ACTU model or any other, but made it clear the minimum wage, as it was currently set, was no longer adequate. It would either be increased using a new mechanism or replaced by a living wage.

"The minimum wage is no longer a living wage," he said. "And the current framework simply doesn't give adequate consideration to contemporary cost of living pressures that working people are battling.

"Our goal should be a real, living wage - effectively raising the pay of all Australians, particularly the 2.3 million who depend upon the minimum rates in the awards."

The Turnbull government believes its company tax cuts, if fully legislated, will funnel through in the form of more jobs and better pay, but Mr Shorten ended any prospect of Labor ever supporting the cuts. And he again refused to rule out reversing the cuts the government has already managed to legislate - a reduced rate for businesses with turnovers capped at $50 million.

"Perhaps Mr Turnbull and co genuinely believe that if you give corporations everything they want, the world will be a better place," Mr Shorten said.

"But for the life of me I don't see how dumping a big truckful of taxpayer funds into the pockets of multinationals in the form of a tax cut is going to help ordinary people."

He suggested that the better way to ensure higher wages was to boost the minimum wage and change the rules for enterprise bargaining which, he said, was "on life support".

He indicated a Labor government would take aim at provisions which allow employers to terminate agreements and force workers back to award minimums.

"In the last financial year, terminations were more than double the long-term average and, in that process, all the carefully negotiated conditions are wiped away," he said. "Existing agreements should stay in place until they're renegotiated by mutual agreement."

One business source said the speech "is simply Bill's hit list for the next election and that can be summarised as a war on business".

The plan to take aim at enterprise bargaining rules was first flagged in August last year by shadow employment minister Brendan O'Connor who said declining rates of collective bargaining and union membership were contributing to low wage growth and job insecurity, and that workplace bargaining power had tilted too far in favour of employers.

That speech alarmed business groups. After Mr Shorten spoke, Australian Industry Group chief executive Innes Willox said the proposals were unwelcome amid signs of economic recovery and strong jobs growth.

"The last thing employers need is further restrictions and greater rigidity in the workplace. Employers need an IR system they can work with and that they have faith in and that is not designed to deliver one-sided outcomes," he said.

"We hope to continue conversations with the opposition about developing policy which provides grounds for growth and fairness."

This, he said, must include a lower company tax rate for Australia to remain competitive as other nations, including the US under Donald Trump, lowered their rates.

He also took issue with Mr Shorten's claim that the termination of agreements by employers was spiralling.

"The unions are always arguing that a large number of enterprise agreements are being unilaterally terminated by employers. This is wrong," he said. "The Fair Work Commission's statistics show that only a minuscule proportion of agreements are terminated in proceedings contested between employers and unions. Statistics submitted by the Fair Work Commission to a Senate inquiry last year showed that less than 3 per cent of applications to terminate enterprise agreements were contested. The vast majority of enterprise agreements that are terminated relate to projects or contracts that have been completed."

James Pearson of the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry said the previous Labor government had introduced the IR laws that frustrated both the labour movement and business.

"It's important that any review by a future Labor government not simply adopt the prescription of the trade union movement. For Australian business to stay competitive in an increasingly competitive world, we need an IR system that is fit for purpose and that means the views of business must be given equal weight to those of unions."

Mr Shorten also singled out private health insurers, saying the latest 4 per cent increase in premiums, while the lowest for years, was still unacceptable. "I put private health insurance, the big end, the big multinationals, the big profitable companies on notice - business as usual doesn't work. If you are getting a $6 billion subsidy from the taxpayer yet you're making record profits, yet the prices are going up and the exclusions are going up, well that's a problem.

"Private health insurance, I want to save it. You're not going to save it by increasing the prices the way they are. They've gone up for families a thousand bucks since the Liberals got in."

HEADLINE: ASIC hits Comyn with rate rigging
TEXT:
A day after being appointed the Commonwealth Bank of Australia's new chief executive, Matt Comyn has been drawn into the BBSW rate rigging saga by the corporate regulator beginning court proceedings against the bank.

Mr Comyn will have to defend the bank against Australian Securities and Investments Commission allegations that the bank's employees sought to manipulate a key benchmark to the benefit of the bank at the expense of its customers and other banks.

Documents filed with the Federal Court on Tuesday claim that Commonwealth Bank traders sought to manipulate the interbank lending rate on February 3, February 9 and March 15, 2012.

ASIC alleges that during the relevant period the bank "had a practice of" trading prime bank bills with the purpose of moving the rate to its advantage or to the advantage of one of its business units.

A spokesperson for Commonwealth Bank said it would dispute the claim and was planning to contest the allegations. The bank said it had fully co-operated with ASIC's investigation over the last two years. A directions hearing has been scheduled for Friday in Melbourne's Federal Court on William Street.

The surprise announcement came 24 hours after the bank's chairman, Catherine Livingstone, told media Mr Comyn was unlikely to have to deal with any new scandals.

On Monday the bank submitted a 50-page report detailing instances of misconduct at the bank stretching back 10 years to the Hayne royal commission.

A report into the governance, culture and accountability frameworks at the bank is due to be handed to the banking regulator the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority tomorrow.

It will also occupy much of the incoming ASIC chairman James Shipton's time, who is due to start in the job on Thursday, February 1.

Commonwealth Bank is the last of the big four banks to be drawn into the scandal after ANZ and NAB settled with the regulator at the last minute.

ANZ and NAB paid $50 million each to settle the case with the payment consisting of a fine, costs and a donation. The fine component amounted to around $1 million per breach.

Westpac chose to fight the allegations and is awaiting a judgment from Justice Jonathan Beach.

The action follows rumours that the regulator was preparing to take action against the bank in the lead-up to Christmas following two months of hearings in ASIC's case against Westpac.

Westpac traders including Sophie 'The Perfumed Steamroller' Johnston, Colin 'The Rat' Roden, Patrick 'The Sherriff' Stokes and Daniel 'Bench' Park were among those to give evidence.

The roles and identities of Commonwealth Bank's traders of bank bills including Garfield 'Bad Kitty' Lee and Mark 'The Powerful Owl' Hulme were also revealed during the trial.

Mr Hulme sat alongside Mr Roden on the Benchmarks Committee of the Australian Financial Markets Association, the body responsible for guidelines around the setting of BBSW.

Bloomberg chats between Commonwealth Bank's Mr Lee and Westpac's Mr Roden saw the two joke about the market which Mr Lee described as a casino. In another exchange read to the court, Mr Roden gave Mr Lee advice on how Commonwealth Bank should structure its operations. Mr Lee is no longer with the bank.

The regulator's delay in instigating proceedings against Australia's biggest bank may relate to the relatively small number of breaches the regulator has identified. NAB was alleged by the regulator to have committed 50 breaches, ANZ 44 breaches and Westpac 16 breaches.

NAB would ultimately admit to just 12 instances of attempted unconscionable conduct and ANZ just 10. Each bank paid a $10 million fine, $20 million of costs and a $20 million donation to a financial literacy fund. The settlements were approved by Justice Jaygot late in 2017 who lashed the banks for thier role in the scandal.

HEADLINE: Shorten channels Kevin 07 in a tilt at the status quo
TEXT:
A new year, a new agenda.

Labor under Bill Shorten has successfully managed to leapfrog the federal political agenda of the Coalition in the past with a series of brave and politically savvy policy calls on issues like negative gearing.

On Tuesday at the National Press Club, the Opposition Leader moved to do it again.

Out went the issues on which he was able to create both product differentiation with, and political difficulty for, the government in 2017 - same-sex marriage, power prices, a banking royal commission - which the government has now largely neutralised.

In came issues close to Labor's traditional heartland. In the process, however, Shorten appeared to revive the plays of Kevin '07, albeit updated by a decade.

Shorten himself invoked Rudd in his speech, commending the former prime minister for his courage in making the national apology to Indigenous Australians 10 years ago.

"As Prime Minister, Kevin had the courage to tell the truth about history, say sorry to the injustices and indignities inflicted upon our First Australians and, indeed, it is courage and imagination that I wish to talk about today," he said.

"That is what I think Australians are looking for in 2018."

But it was not just Rudd's courage that Shorten was invoking, but a very familiar agenda, even if for the moment the policy specifics remain unclear.

Climate change; cost of living; government integrity; industrial relations. These were at the heart of Rudd's Kevin 07 campaign.

His advocacy of a federal integrity commission will be both popular, and a point of difference with the government.

Ramping up the pressure on the private health insurance industry will also ring true with voters (and send a chill through the industry) as a central cost of living issue - and one that government actually has more power to address than Rudd's war on petrol prices, or Tony Abbott's promise on power prices.

Shorten pointed to premiums rising at twice the rate of wages, and 20 per cent profits in the sector - twice as big as the much scorned banks - before pointedly referring to a multibillion-dollar government subsidy the sector enjoys.

(It was striking that, in his speech, Shorten listed rising health costs, house prices and rising rents and "household bills" but made no direct reference to the surging power prices that have so dominated recent political debate.)

But the really interesting political and policy move by Shorten is on industrial relations.

Where Rudd was exploiting the overstep of John Howard's WorkChoices in 2007, a combination of rising prices but static wages allows Shorten to take the industrial relations debate back to its historic roots.

Echoing an ACTU campaign, the Opposition Leader is not targeting the minimum wage but the idea of what is a living wage.

For the historically aware, this takes us right back to the 1907 Harvester judgment, which lay at the foundations of the centralised wages fixing system.

In a modern context it offers the opportunity to press political buttons for a generation (possibly several generations) of voters who may not know about our industrial relations history but know they don't feel they are being paid enough to live on.

Shorten is linking this with questions about the very credibility of the enterprise bargaining system, charging that it is employers who are effectively abandoning the system rather than workers; and with a charge that productivity gains are not being reflected in wage outcomes.

These charges make his industrial relations attack a profound one that challenges not just the Coalition's industrial relations agenda but the status quo of the past couple of decades, and extends it to one that goes beyond a simple institutional reinforcement of his trade union base.

Laura Tingle is The Australian Financial Review's political editor.
